::: notes
Today we’re focusing on bicycling, not just as a mode of transportation, but as something that’s been deeply shaped by a combination of both technological innovations and the cities themselves—their streets, their politics, and their priorities.

One thing I want to flag right away is that bicycling’s history in cities is not a steady success story to be sure. It’s a story of moments when bikes were new and thought of as novelties, moments when they were pushed aside and not thought of as legitimate transportation, and moments when cities tried to bring them back.

As we go through this lecture, we’re going to look at bicycling alongside other modes, especially automobiles, and ask why biking worked well in some periods and places—and why it struggled in others.

As with all of these presentations, the goal isn’t to memorize dates or technologies. Rather the key is to better understand how decisions about these unique forms of mobility has street space and infrastructure shape what kinds of movement feel normal, safe, or even possible.

Keep that framing in mind as we move through the periods—you’ll see that the bicycle itself changes as well as the city around it.
:::

---

## Periods of Urban Bicycling
:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
-   Period 1: Proto-Bicycles & Mechanical Curiosity (1816–1860s)
-   Period 2: Safety Bicycles & The First Urban Cycling Boom (1870s–1900)
-   Period 3: Cycling as a Pre-Automobile Urban Mode (1900–1930s)
-   Period 4: Automobile Ascendancy & Cycling Marginalization (1930s–1960s)
-   Period 5: Oil Crisis & Environmental Reawakening (1970s)
-   Period 6: Information Technologies & Sharing Economies (2000s–2010s)
-   Period 7: Rise of Electric Micromobility Vehicles  (2020s-Present)
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

### Sources

!['Cycling 1839-1939' book issued by John Player & Sons (1939).<br>I purchased it at an outdoor flea market while on a UK trip in summer 2025.](images/players_cycling_book_1816_1939.jpg)

![The Mechanical Hourse: How the Bicycle Reshaped American Life (2016)](images/the_mechanical_horse_margaret_guroff.png)

![Planning for Shared Mobility (2016)](images/pas_planning_for_shared_mobility.png)

:::

::::

::: notes
We can broadly and somewhat arbitrarily organize the history of urban bicycling into seven periods.

The first period, in the early 1800s through the 1860s, bikes weren’t really “transportation” yet. Things like the hobby bike were more experiments than practical vehicles. People were basically testing the idea that you could move faster than walking without a horse. Cities weren’t built for that yet, so these early bikes mostly showed us what the potential for human-powered mobility while simultaneously exposing the limitations of urban environments and infrastructure.

That changes pretty dramatically toward the end of the 19th century with the safety bicycle. This is the first real moment when biking starts to matter in everyday urban life. People begin to use bikes to get around, roads improve because cyclists demand smoother surfaces, and biking briefly becomes a normal way to move through cities and, to some extent, rural areas.

In the early 1900s, biking fits naturally into city life. Streets are slower, distances are short, and bikes coexist with pedestrians and streetcars. What’s important at this time is that biking works without modern bike lanes—not because it’s perfect, but because cities are compact and speeds are low.

Then things start to shift. From about the 1890s into the early 20th century, streets become crowded with everything at once—people walking, bikes, streetcars, and cars like the chaotic scene you examined in that famous 1906 San Francisco Market Street film. This is when streets turn into contested spaces, and decisions start getting made about who they’re really for.

By the 1920s, the car wins that fight. Streets are redesigned by transportation engineers who focused on speed and throughput, levels of service while biking and walking get pushed aside, and over time they’re treated as unsafe or outdated. A lot of the safety and equity problems we talk about today trace back to this period.

Starting in the 1960s, people begin to push back. Traffic deaths rise, pollution gets worse, and cities start questioning whether car dominance makes sense. Early biking and walking advocates don’t win big right away, but they change how people start to think about streets. In some areas of the world such as western Europe (Denmark, the Netherlands), biking makes a big comeback.

From the 1990s to today, biking comes back into the conversation in many more industrialized cities, this time tied to sustainability, health, and climate change. But it’s important to remember—we’re not going back to pre-car cities within these later periods. We’re trying to reintroduce biking into systems that are still mostly designed around cars yet can be retrofitted to allow for multiple transportation options.

So as we go through these periods, keep asking: What changed about bicycling technology? What changed about the street? Who was the street designed for? And how did design choices and advocacy affect who felt safe or welcome moving through the city?
:::

---

## Period 1: Proto-Bicycles & Mechanical Curiosity (1816–1860s)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
### Key Developments
- Early innovations in cycling were essentially scooters (aka "hobby horse", "dandy horse", "running machine", "draisine-style" or modern "balance bikes") with no pedals
- Lever-driven cycles preceded pedal-driven velocipedes
- Foot pedals added to the front wheel as part of "boneshaker" bicycle
- These early transportation technologies were essential mechanical experiments that bridged walking and cycling and represented the first practical attempts of human-powered wheeled personal transport


### Urban Transportation Relevance
- Early cycles often made of wood (not mass produced) that offered limited everyday use
- Largely used in parks, promenades, and wide boulevards (e.g., Hyde Park, Regent's Park) for recreational travel among the elite (mostly upper-class men) who could afford them
- They offered demonstrations of modernity and a break from animal-powered transport

### Sustainability Significance
- Established the potential of zero-emission, human-powered mobility
- Laid groundwork for later urban and rural adoption
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

![Pedestrian hobby horse. (1816)](images/1816_pedestrian_hobby_horse.png)

![Lady's hobby horse. (1818)](images/1818_lady_hobby_horse.png)

![Lever-driven bicycle. (1818)](images/1865_lever_driven_bicycle.png)

![Jardin du Luxembourg. Gentry Publishers. (1818)](images/1818_draisine_style_bike.webp)

![Johnson's Pedestrian Hobby Horse Riding School (1819)](images/1819_draisine_riding_school.webp)

!["The Horse Dealer" (1819). British Museum](images/1819_cycle_horse_dealer.webp)

![The "boneshaker" bicycle (1867)](images/1865_michaux_boneshaker.png)
:::
::::


::: notes

In this first period, it’s important to reset our expectations. These early “bicycles” weren’t really bikes in the modern sense. Most of them were basically scooters—what you’ll see called hobby horses, dandy horses, running machines, or draisine-style bikes. There were no pedals, no chains, and no gears. Riders pushed along with their feet, very similar to modern balance bikes for kids.

Before pedals became standard, there were a lot of experiments. Some designs used levers, others attached pedals directly to the front wheel, which led to what were known as “boneshakers.” These weren’t comfortable or efficient, but that’s not really the point. This period is about mechanical experimentation—figuring out how balance, steering, and speed might work on two wheels.

From an urban transportation perspective, these early bikes had pretty limited everyday use. They were often made of wood, not mass-produced, and expensive. As a result, they were mostly used by wealthier men, and usually in places like parks, promenades, and wide boulevards—spaces where riding wouldn’t interfere too much with pedestrians or horse traffic.

What they really did was signal modernity. These machines represented a clear break from animal-powered transport and hinted at a future where individuals could move faster using their own energy alone.

From a sustainability perspective, this period is important even though the technology wasn’t practical yet. It established the idea that human-powered, zero-emission mobility was possible. Even if these early devices didn’t transform cities, they laid the conceptual groundwork for later bicycles that absolutely would.

So for this period, the takeaway isn’t widespread adoption—it’s the moment when walking began to blur into wheeled personal transport, setting the stage for everything that comes next.

:::

---

## Period 2: Safety Bicycles & The First Urban Cycling Boom (1870s–1900)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
### Key Developments
- Introduction of chain drive systems, pneumatic tires, and mass-production techniques transformed the bicycle into a reliable, comfortable, and widely accessible technology.
- These innovations dramatically reduced costs, allowing bicycles to become affordable to broad segments of the urban population and enabling rapid diffusion across cities.

### Urban Transportation Relevance
- With improved reliability and comfort, bicycling emerged as a practical mode of daily urban travel rather than a recreational novelty.
- Organized cyclists played an influential role in advocating for smoother road surfaces and early standards for street design and maintenance.

### Sustainability Significance
- Bicycling represented the first large-scale urban transportation mode capable of supporting daily mobility while producing virtually no direct carbon emissions.
- The bicycle expanded personal mobility and access to urban opportunities while requiring minimal materials, energy, and space compared to animal- or motor-powered transport.

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

![The "Ordinary" bicycle (1880)](images/1882_the_ordinary.png)

![The "Safety" bicycle (1885)](images/1885_safety_bicycle.png)

![Good Roads Illinois (1892)](images/good_roads_illinois.jpg)

![Good Roads Illinois Article #1 (1892)](images/good_roads_illinois_example_01.jpg)

![Good Roads Illinois Article #2 (1892)](images/good_roads_illinois_example_02.jpg)

:::
::::

::: notes
Despite a brief decline in the 1820s due to poor road conditions and sidewalk bans, the bicycle saw a transformative resurgence in the late 1860s and early 1870s.

The ordinary, more commonly known as the high-wheel bicycle, arrived and began to be manufactured in the United States in the late 1870s. This period was a milestone in bicycle development that prompted the formation of the first bicycle clubs and a renewed enforcement of riding bans in cities like Boston and New York. These machines were the first bicycles capable of being ridden outdoors for significant distances, a major advancement over their predecessors. 

In the United States, the high-wheeler was popularized by Colonel Albert A. Pope, whose Columbia Bicycle company adapted the "American system of manufacture" to produce these bikes using machine tools for uniform parts rather than individual artisanship. These machines remained the standard for serious cyclists until the advent of the low-profile "safety bicycle" in 1887, which eventually made cycling accessible to a mainstream audience.

The bicycle was beginning to be viewed broadly as a tool for the "annihilation of space and time" for short urban distances. So while earlier inventions like railroads shrunk the countryside, the bicycle was seen as the first machine adequate for shrinking the city, providing an efficient, door-to-door alternative to expensive horses and crowded stagecoaches.

So it was really in this second period when the bicycle stops being a mechanical curiosity and starts to look like a serious transportation technology. A few key innovations come together here: the chain drive, pneumatic tires, and mass production. Each of these matters on its own, but together they completely transform how bicycles function in everyday life.

Another especially important transition during this period was the shift from the *ordinary* or *high-wheeler* bicycle to the *safety bicycle* around 1887. Earlier bicycles were fast but unstable, hard to mount, and frankly dangerous for most people. The safety bicycle—lower to the ground, with equal-sized wheels and a chain-driven rear wheel—dramatically reduced the risk of falls while making riding easier and more intuitive. That change alone opens bicycling up to a much broader population, including women, older riders, and people who weren’t athletic thrill-seekers. 

At the same time, pneumatic tires make riding far more comfortable, especially on rough urban streets. You no longer need ideal conditions to ride a bike. Combine that with factory-based mass production, and suddenly bicycles become cheaper, standardized, and widely available. This is when we see bicycles spreading rapidly through cities rather than remaining a niche or elite product.

From an urban transportation perspective, this is the moment when bicycling becomes practical for daily travel. People start using bikes to get to work, run errands, and move across the city efficiently. Cyclists also begin organizing, forming clubs and advocacy groups that push for smoother roads, better maintenance, and early street design standards. In a real sense, cyclists are among the first modern road users demanding infrastructure improvements.

From a sustainability standpoint, this period is especially significant. The bicycle becomes the first transportation mode capable of supporting everyday urban mobility at scale while producing virtually no direct emissions. It expands personal freedom and access to jobs and services, but does so using very little energy, material, or space—especially when compared to horse-drawn transport or, later, automobiles.

So this period sets a critical foundation: the bicycle is no longer a novelty. It’s affordable, reliable, and safe enough to function as a true urban transportation system—and that has lasting implications for how cities think about mobility, infrastructure, and sustainability.

:::

---

## Period 3: Cycling as a Pre-Automobile Urban Mode (1900–1930s)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
### Key Developments
- By the early 20th century, bicycling had become a routine part of everyday life across much of Europe and North America, used by workers, students, and families for regular urban travel.  
- Bicycles operated alongside walking and streetcar systems, forming an integrated urban mobility environment in which multiple modes shared street space without rigid separation.

### Urban Transportation Relevance
- Cities during this period remained largely human-scaled, with short trip distances, dense development, and active ground-floor uses that made cycling an efficient and natural choice for daily travel.  
- Bicycles functioned both as standalone commute modes and as feeders to streetcar and rail systems, extending the reach of transit and enabling flexible door-to-door mobility.

### Sustainability Significance
- This period demonstrates a balanced multimodal transportation system that existed prior to automobile dominance, where mobility needs were met without high energy consumption or emissions.  
- Cycling reinforced compact urban development patterns and local accessibility, supporting cities that relied more on proximity and human movement than on speed or vehicle capacity.

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

![World champion bicycle racer Marshall "Major" Taylor (1899)](images/1899_major_taylor_documentary.png)

![Six-day bicycle racing (1903)](images/1903_six_day_bicycle_racing.png)

![Multimodal scene down Market Street in San Francisco (1906)](images/1906_market_street_sf_bicycle.png)

![Women, children engaged in rural cycling](images/rural_cycling.png)

:::
::::

::: notes

By the turn of the 20th century, the "bicycle mania" of the 1890s had largely collapsed, with membership in organizations like the League of American Wheelmen plummeting and the social elite moving on to new fads. However, this did not mean the bicycle disappeared; instead, it underwent a critical "demotion" from a high-status toy to a "perfect machine of great practical utility" that was now within the reach of the common worker's purse. While the fashionable crowds vanished, hundreds of thousands of urban workers in North America and Europe continued to integrate the bicycle into their daily lives as a reliable, affordable form of transportation. This era marked the bicycle's transition from a recreational novelty to a standardized urban commute mode.

During the early 20th century, cities remained human-scaled and dense, providing an urban form that was naturally conducive to cycling. In these dense, mixed-use neighborhoods, the bicycle did not exist in isolation but functioned as part of a balanced multimodal system. Bicycles shared the streets and coexisted with pedestrians and the expanding networks of streetcars and electric trolleys that had begun to define urban transit in the late 19th century. In this environment, the bicycle served a dual purpose: it acted as a feeder to transit lines, allowing residents to reach streetcar hubs, and it functioned as a standalone mode for door-to-door commutes.

The sustainability of this period is significant because it demonstrates an efficient transportation framework that existed before the dominance of the automobile. Because the bicycle provided high levels of local accessibility, it reinforced compact development patterns and helped "shrink the city" by providing a level of personal mobility that stagecoaches and germy, crowded transit could not match. Unlike the expensive and feed-dependent horse, the bicycle was a "mechanical horse" that required no fodder, making it a sustainable and less expensive alternative for the urban masses. This period serves as a historical blueprint for a city where various modes of transport—walking, cycling, and transit—work in concert to maintain a functional, human-centric urban environment.

:::

## Period 4: Automobile Ascendancy and Cycling Marginalization (1930s–1960s)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

### Key Developments
- Rapid motorization reshaped daily travel as automobiles became more affordable and widely available, coinciding with suburbanization and the decentralization of housing, jobs, and services.  
- Road design and traffic engineering increasingly prioritized vehicle speed, capacity, and throughput, leading to wider streets, higher design speeds, and the removal of street features that supported slower, human-scale movement.

### Urban Transportation Relevance
- Cycling was progressively reframed as unsafe, inefficient, or obsolete in the context of faster and more complex traffic environments, and increasingly associated with children, recreation, or poverty rather than everyday mobility.  
- Dedicated cycling infrastructure that had existed informally or implicitly in earlier periods disappeared, and cyclists lost political influence as transportation planning became dominated by automotive and highway interests.

### Sustainability Significance
- This period represents a major missed opportunity, as cities displaced one of the most energy-efficient and space-efficient transportation modes in favor of energy-intensive automobility.  
- The shift toward car-oriented urban systems laid the groundwork for long-term challenges, including traffic congestion, rising greenhouse gas emissions, air pollution, physical inactivity, and widening public health and equity disparities.

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

![Italian Velocino bicycle (1935)](images/1935_novelty_italian_cycle_smoking_rider.png)

![Horizontal bicycle (1933)](images/1933_horizontal_recumbant_bicycle.png)

![Touring tandem (1930s)](images/1939_touring_tandem.png)

![International cycle touring (1938)](images/1938_international_cycling_tour.png)

![American "motorbike" (1939)](images/1939_american_motor_bicycle.png)

![Detailed diorama from Futurama exhibit at New York City's World's Fair (1939)](images/1939_futurama_diorama_detail.jpg)

:::
::::

::: notes

The period between the 1930s and the 1960s was defined by a profound irony: the bicycle, which had effectively paved the way for the automobile, was pushed to the margins by the very culture it helped create. Technological innovations originally developed for bicycles—such as pneumatic tires, ball bearings, and differential gears—became the mechanical foundation for early automobile chassis. Furthermore, the political lobbying of the "Good Roads" movement, led by cyclists in the late 19th century, provided the initial marked, mapped, and paved routes that automobile tourists would later dominate. As motorization and suburbanization accelerated during this period, travel was reshaped as automobiles became more affordable, coinciding with a decentralization of housing and jobs that made car-free living increasingly difficult.

During this era, urban transportation was radically reshaped as road design and traffic engineering began to prioritize vehicle speed, capacity, and throughput. This focus on the automobile led to wider streets and higher design speeds, which necessitated the removal of street features that supported slower, human-scale movement. Consequently, the dedicated cycling infrastructure of the previous generation was dismantled; for example, hundreds of miles of separate side-paths were paved over as roads were widened to accommodate cars. By the mid-twentieth century, the bicycle had lost its political influence, and on-street cycling became increasingly dangerous because roads were built or rebuilt with only cars in mind, lacking even basic safety features like curb cuts.

As the physical environment changed, cycling was progressively reframed as unsafe, inefficient, or obsolete. It lost its status as a primary mode of everyday mobility and became associated almost exclusively with children, recreation, or poverty. By the 1950s and 60s, cycling was widely dismissed as "kid stuff"; many teenagers refused to be "caught dead" on a bike, often walking long distances to school to avoid the perceived embarrassment of using a vehicle associated with childhood. This social marginalization was reinforced by a medical community that often warned adults that vigorous exercise after age thirty was "hurtful" or even "slow suicide".

From a sustainability perspective, this period represents a major missed opportunity. Cities displaced one of the most energy-efficient and space-efficient transportation modes in favor of energy-intensive automobility. This shift laid the groundwork for long-term challenges, including chronic traffic congestion and air pollution. Before federal emission standards were introduced in 1965, automobiles spewed smoke that created thick "smog episodes," leading the US Surgeon General to warn that society was creating an "incredible disharmony in nature". Furthermore, the sedentary, car-centric lifestyle contributed to a population that was "plumper" and less physically active than previous generations, setting the stage for the public health and equity disparities that define many modern urban environments.

:::

---

## Period 5: Oil Crises and Environmental Reawakening (1970s)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

### Key Developments
- The 1973 oil crisis exposed the economic and geopolitical vulnerability of automobile-dependent transportation systems, prompting governments and the public to reconsider energy-intensive travel patterns.  
- In response, grassroots cycling and pedestrian activism emerged—particularly in Northern European cities—where citizens organized protests and campaigns demanding safer streets, reduced traffic speeds, and greater investment in non-motorized transport.

### Urban Transportation Relevance
- Cities such as Amsterdam and Copenhagen began to reverse decades of automobile-oriented planning by reinvesting in cycling infrastructure, including protected bike lanes, traffic calming measures, and network continuity.  
- During this period, cycling was reframed as a practical and reliable mode of daily transportation rather than a recreational activity, especially for short urban trips and commuting.

### Sustainability Significance
- For the first time, cycling was explicitly linked to broader concerns about energy security, environmental degradation, and urban livability, rather than framed solely around efficiency or convenience.  
- This era marked an early articulation of cycling as a climate-responsive urban policy tool, laying the conceptual and political groundwork for later sustainability and climate-action–oriented transportation planning.

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

![The inaugural issue of Bicycling! magazine in 1971 marked the emergence of cycling as a modern lifestyle and transportation movement in the U.S., blending advocacy, equipment guidance, and practical riding advice at the dawn of the bike boom and early environmental era.](images/1971_bicycle_magazine.jpg)

![In 1971, Bicycling! magazine ran an early feature on Major Taylor, helping reintroduce his legacy to a new generation of riders and advocates.](images/1971_bicycle_magazine_major_taylor_article.jpg)

![The Raleigh Twenty was a compact, 20-inch–wheel folding bicycle gained popularity in the early 1970s, designed for practicality and easy storage while maintaining the ride quality of a full-sized utility bike.](images/1974_raleigh_twenty_folding_bike.jpg)

![During the 1970s and 80s, the Danish Cyclists’ Federation organised a number of demonstrations. Photo: Bo Hansen, Danish Cyclists’ Federation’s archive](images/1970s_danish_bicycle_protests.png)

:::
::::

::: notes

In October 1973, a major geopolitical shift occurred when Arab oil-producing countries cut off petroleum exports to the United States, exposing the profound economic and geopolitical vulnerability of automobile-dependent transportation. As gas prices quadrupled and drivers faced massive lines at the pumps, the "mechanical horse" suddenly regained its status as a highly practical alternative to the car. This energy crisis served as a catalyst for governments and the public to reconsider energy-intensive travel patterns in favor of "good ol’ American leg power".

This period saw a surge in grassroots activism as citizens organized to demand safer, more human-scaled urban environments. While this was particularly prominent in Northern European cities like Amsterdam and Copenhagen, where protesters campaigned for reduced traffic speeds, similar movements took hold in the United States. In 1971, activists in Manhattan organized rides to demand dedicated bike lanes, while groups like Friends for Bikecology framed cycling as a way for individuals to take personal responsibility for the state of the planet. These efforts led cities to begin reversing decades of car-centric planning by reinvesting in cycling infrastructure, including protected lanes and traffic calming measures.

The resulting "Great American Bicycle Boom" effectively reframed the bicycle as a reliable mode of daily transportation for adults rather than just "kid stuff". By 1971, 86 percent of bicycle sales were to adults—a total reversal from just years prior—and between 1972 and 1974, bicycles actually outsold cars in the United States. For the first time since the early 20th century, the bicycle was recognized as the swiftest way to navigate congested urban centers, with commuters finding they could consistently outpace city buses and cars on short trips.

Finally, the 1970s marked a critical sustainability milestone by explicitly linking cycling to energy security, environmental health, and urban livability. Amidst the rise of the environmental movement and the first Earth Day in 1970, the non-polluting bicycle became a "symbolic savior of the planet". This era provided the first articulation of cycling as a climate-responsive urban policy tool, establishing the conceptual and political foundation for the sustainability and climate-action planning that defines modern transportation discourse.

:::

--- 

## Period 6: Institutionalization of Cycling Policy (1980s–1990s)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

### Key Developments
- During the 1980s and 1990s, many cities began to move beyond ad hoc or recreational cycling facilities and instead developed formal, connected bike lane networks that were planned at the citywide or regional scale.  
- Cycling was increasingly integrated into transportation planning and traffic engineering practices, with design standards, guidelines, and professional expertise emerging to address cyclist safety, facility design, and network performance.

### Urban Transportation Relevance
- In this period, cycling became a deliberate and recognized component of urban mobility systems rather than an afterthought, with planners and engineers accounting for cyclists in roadway design, signal timing, and street reconstruction projects.  
- Empirical evidence began to accumulate showing that safety improves when cycling infrastructure is continuous, legible, and physically separated from high-speed motor traffic, reinforcing the importance of network-based approaches.

### Sustainability Significance
- This era demonstrates that cycling levels are shaped primarily by policy choices and infrastructure design rather than cultural preference alone, challenging the notion that high cycling rates are unique to specific countries or populations.  
- By supporting mode shift away from private automobiles, institutionalized cycling policy reinforced cycling’s role in reducing greenhouse gas emissions, improving air quality, and enhancing overall urban livability.

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

![The CROW Design Manual for Bicycle Traffic was first formally published in 1993, building on Dutch cycling research and practice developed throughout the 1970s and 1980s. The guide is now widely used and referenced across Europe and internationally.](images/1993_crow_design_guide.jpg)

![Beginning in the 1970s and accelerating through the 1990s, the Netherlands developed a national intercity cycling network by systematically connecting towns with direct, protected routes—later formalized as high-quality bicycle highways—integrating cycling into regional travel rather than limiting it to local trips. Travel route by C. Scott Smith (2024)](images/1990s_netherlands_intercity_bike_infrastructure_01.png)

![Bike path outside of Utrecht, Netherlands. Photo: C. Scott Smith (2024)](images/1990s_netherlands_intercity_bike_infrastructure_02.jpg)

![Bike path outside of Gouda, Netherlands. Photo: C. Scott Smith (2024)](images/1990s_netherlands_intercity_bike_infrastructure.jpg)

![Bike path along North Sea, Netherlands. Photo: C. Scott Smith (2024)](images/1990s_netherlands_intercity_bike_infrastructure_03.jpg)

![The Illinois Prairie Path, established beginning in 1963 on a former Chicago, Aurora & Elgin interurban rail corridor, was one of the nation’s earliest rail-to-trail projects and helped pioneer off-street bicycling in the Chicago region. Photo: C. Scott Smith (2024)](images/1990s_rails_to_trails_prairie_path_illinois.jpg)

:::
::::

::: notes

By the 1980s and 1990s, the bicycle had decisively shed its "just-for-kids" image, a transformation that began during the great boom of the 1970s. While earlier decades treated cycling facilities as ad hoc or purely recreational, this period marked a shift toward formal, connected bike lane networks planned at citywide or regional scales. An early milestone of this institutionalization was seen in cities like Manhattan, which introduced its first on-street bicycle lanes in 1978, signaling a move toward integrating cyclists into the existing urban grid. This transition reflected a growing recognition that cycling could serve as a deliberate and recognized component of urban mobility rather than a mere afterthought.

This era also saw cycling become increasingly integrated into the professional practices of transportation planning and traffic engineering. In previous decades, on-street cycling in the United States was notoriously dangerous because roads were built or rebuilt with only cars in mind. However, during the 1980s and 90s, planners and engineers began accounting for cyclists in roadway design and signal timing. A significant technical advancement for urban cycling accessibility occurred with the passage of the Americans with Disabilities Act in 1990, which led to the widespread installation of curb cuts. While intended for accessibility, these features removed a major physical barrier for cyclists who had previously struggled with the "obstacle course" of high curbs and car-centric street design.

The sustainability significance of this period lies in the accumulation of empirical evidence showing that safety and ridership levels are primarily shaped by policy choices and infrastructure design. The sources note that before this institutionalization, cyclists were often vulnerable to both high-speed traffic and urban crime, particularly in densely built environments. By moving toward networks that were continuous, legible, and physically separated from motor traffic, cities proved that high cycling rates were not merely a result of "cultural preference" but a response to safe and efficient infrastructure. By supporting a mode shift away from private automobiles, these institutionalized policies reinforced the bicycle's role in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and enhancing overall urban livability.

:::

## Period 7: Information Technologies, Equity and Sharing Economies (2000s–2010s)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

### Key Developments
- During the 2000s and 2010s, cycling became increasingly embedded in climate change mitigation strategies as cities and regions sought to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from transportation, the largest and fastest-growing source of emissions in many countries.  
- At the same time, a growing body of public health research linked active transportation to reduced rates of chronic disease, improved mental health, and lower health care costs, providing an empirical foundation for cycling investments beyond transportation efficiency alone.  
- Bike sharing systems expanded rapidly across Europe, North America, and the Global South, enabled by digital technologies, GPS tracking, and new business models that made short-term bicycle access easy and scalable.

### Urban Transportation Relevance
- Cycling was explicitly positioned as a policy response to multiple urban challenges at once, including traffic congestion, air pollution, climate emissions, and rising rates of physical inactivity and chronic disease.  
- Bike share systems lowered barriers to cycling by reducing the need for personal bike ownership, extending the reach of transit systems, and enabling first- and last-mile connections in dense urban environments.

### Sustainability Significance
- This period produced a strong and widely accepted evidence base demonstrating cycling’s triple-bottom-line benefits, including environmental gains through emissions reduction, health benefits through increased physical activity, and economic benefits through lower infrastructure and health care costs.  
- Equity and access became increasingly central to cycling policy debates, with greater attention to the spatial distribution of infrastructure, affordability, and the inclusion of historically underserved communities in planning and investment decisions.

:::

::::


::: notes
During the 2000s and 2010s, the bicycle’s role in society underwent a significant transformation, evolving from the "symbolic savior of the planet" seen in the 1970s into a central pillar of global climate change mitigation strategies. As transportation became recognized as one of the largest and fastest-growing sources of greenhouse gas emissions, cities and regions began to embed cycling into formal policy to meet emissions-reduction targets. This shift mirrors the historical "annihilation of space and time," where the bicycle—once heralded in 1869 as a tool to "shrink the city" for short distances—is now utilized to shrink the carbon footprint of urban mobility.

This era also saw an explosion in public health research that provided an empirical foundation for cycling investments. While mid-20th-century doctors often dismissed adult exercise as "hurtful," the pioneering work of figures like Dr. Paul Dudley White in the 1950s—who advocated for cycling to prevent heart disease—finally reached its logical conclusion in modern policy. Contemporary research has linked active transportation to lower rates of chronic disease and improved mental health, addressing the legacy of the "plumper and more sedentary" lifestyle that emerged during the automobile’s ascendancy. By framing cycling through a health lens, modern planners have moved beyond simple transportation efficiency to emphasize the triple-bottom-line benefits of environmental, health, and economic gains.

One of the most visible developments of this period was the rapid expansion of bike-sharing systems, enabled by digital technologies and GPS tracking. These systems addressed long-standing historical barriers to cycling, such as the high cost of quality machines and the risk of theft, which had helped end the 1970s bike boom. By providing easy, short-term access, bike-share lowered the threshold for entry and functioned as a "first- and last-mile" connection to transit systems. This technological leap effectively fulfilled the 19th-century vision of the bicycle as a "perfect machine of great practical utility" that is accessible even to those who do not wish to own or store a personal vehicle.

Finally, equity and access became central to the cycling discourse in the 2010s. Early cycling history was dominated by the "well-to-do" and "fashionable citizens" who had the leisure time and resources to adopt new technology. In contrast, modern policy focuses on the spatial distribution of infrastructure and the inclusion of historically underserved communities. This marks a shift from the "elite" beginnings of the hobby-horse and the Ordinary toward a more democratic urban mobility system. Furthermore, the widespread adoption of infrastructure standards—building on the 1990 Americans with Disabilities Act and its introduction of curb cuts—has helped transform the city from a car-centric "obstacle course" into a more inclusive environment for all users.
:::

---

## Period 8: Emergence and Integration of Electric Bikes (2020s-Present)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

### Key Developments
- Rapid growth of electric-assist bicycles (e-bikes), driven by improvements in battery technology, declining costs, and expanded model types ranging from commuter and cargo bikes to adaptive and accessibility-focused designs.  
- Accelerated adoption during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, as cities reallocated street space, expanded bike networks, and individuals sought flexible, socially distanced travel options.  
- Policy recognition of e-bikes as a distinct mobility category, with new regulations, incentives, and pilot programs addressing speed classes, safety, and integration with existing cycling infrastructure.

### Urban Transportation Relevance
- E-bikes significantly extend the feasible distance, speed, and demographic reach of cycling, making biking practical for longer trips, hilly terrain, older adults, and people with physical limitations.  
- They blur the traditional boundary between bicycles and motorized modes, increasingly substituting for short car trips and supporting first- and last-mile connections to transit.  
- Cities begin adapting infrastructure, curb management, and parking policies to accommodate higher cycling volumes, cargo bikes, and mixed-speed bicycle traffic.

### Sustainability Significance
- E-bikes offer substantial emissions reductions by replacing car trips with a mode that consumes a fraction of the energy of even electric automobiles.  
- By expanding who can realistically cycle and for what purposes, e-bikes strengthen the scalability of active transportation as a climate mitigation strategy rather than a niche solution.  
- Their integration raises new equity and sustainability questions—around affordability, access, safety, and regulation—highlighting the need for policy frameworks that ensure e-bikes contribute to inclusive, low-carbon urban mobility systems.

:::

::::

::: notes

In this most recent period, electric bikes really change what cycling can be in cities. E-bikes lower the physical barriers that limited traditional cycling—distance, hills, age, fitness, even time—so biking starts to compete directly with short car trips rather than just walking or transit. Their growth accelerated during the pandemic, when people needed flexible, low-contact ways to get around and cities rapidly expanded bike infrastructure. What’s important here is that e-bikes blur the line between bicycles and motorized modes: they’re still human-scale and energy-efficient, but they extend the range and usefulness of cycling in a way we haven’t seen before. From a planning perspective, this forces cities to rethink infrastructure, speed management, parking, and even freight, as cargo e-bikes begin replacing delivery vans for some trips. From a sustainability standpoint, e-bikes are powerful because they can substitute for car travel at a fraction of the energy and emissions, but they also raise new questions about equity, safety, and regulation that cities are still figuring out. In many ways, this period isn’t just about a new technology—it’s about whether cities can integrate e-bikes in a way that scales active transportation without recreating the problems of automobility.

:::
